story_text.value:
This is a free to play, no sign up required domino rally simulator. You design them with the editor, and then run them in the 3D player. The from-behind "Chase" view is best.

My mum helped develop it - she submitted issue reports direct from the app itself (make it possible to bend the domino tracks, make the playback controls disappear while mouse inactive, add like buttons to the showcase, let me change the backdrop, etc) and the Claude Code session running in the cloud watched, fixed them and on my approval, pushed them live.

I've been making a lot of apps in various sessions which share the same repo. One of them https://www.orgiggly.com/david/aurora (an atmospheric musical loop generator) was plundered to generate a unique soundtrack for each rally (seeded by its name) - which is exactly how the orgiggly platform I built is supposed to work - each app created can make contributions to the next one.

story_text.value:
I use Kuma for a few microservices I’ve built. It’s a simple open source tool for monitoring APIs, ports, websites etc if they are down.

The issue I get is that they are hosted on your own infrastructure, so it doesn’t do you a whole lot of good if your site is down and it takes your Kuma down with it. This also leads to a bunch of false notifications which are annoying.

From what I can tell, people in the GitHub comments are looking for hosted Kuma.

I built DownForReal (largely with LLMs) but what it does is it hosts Kuma and if Kuma is reporting the service down, probes from US, Frankfurt, and Singapore are sent to confirm the outage (looking for 2 out of 3 of the regions).

I’m asking $10 a month or $75 a year.

I’m really just launching this as a service bc I built it for myself.

There is also a simple importer for uptimerobot exports.

title.value: Show HN: DownForReal – Kuma Hosted from 3 regions

story_text.value:
I've always loved flipbooks, the little stick figure running and jumping around the corner of a page. I was curious if I could hi-jack a font file with stick figure glyphs. So I prompted Flipbook Foundry into existence.

Each animated frame of the a stick figure's motion is just a glyph in the font. You can drop {walk} into a paragraph and a stick figure walks right through it, at text size, and the words move aside.

The text reflow runs on Cheng Lou's awesome pretext library, which is fast enough to animate everything performantly.

There's an API for it (framer-motion style, for Svelte / React / plain JS), and the fonts are regular .otf files. Made a little demo page too - check it out and enjoy the swarm!

story_text.value:
Hello HN!

I'd like to share the project I've been working on for the last couple of months.

On microcontrollers with only a few kilobytes of memory (both Flash and SRAM) heatshrink [1] and tamp [2] are the current meta when it comes to decompression of static assets. They are small, configurable, and produce good compression ratio.

However, when random-access workflows are concerned (like extracting a single parameter from a configuration file), both compressors require the exact same window to be allocated. This means that, to decompress a small (4-32 bytes) chunk, memory consumption stays the same as when decompression the entire payload.

blaris is a Windowless LZSS algorithm, meaning that it is LZSS but does not allocate a window. This allows it to reach the same compression ratio (and sometimes even better) as heatshrink and tamp, while keeping memory usage extremely minimal (around 100 bytes of SRAM).

Typical LZ77/LZSS works by copying a byte from the window buffer when resolving a match. Windowless version works by resolving this match using the compressed payload itself - following the chain of matches until it finds a literal run token.

To facilitate this, tokens are split into 3 streams:

1. controls (1 byte per value) - encode either literal run length (1 to 16) or 240 different pairs (match_len, match_distance_log2).

2. literals (1 byte per value) - raw literals.

3. distance bits (bit-packed) - contains bit-packed match offsets.

Because controls are 1 byte and determine the size of the token, we can traverse all 3 streams in both directions, which enables the windowless LZSS!

There are additional optimizations used to speed this up:

1. checkpoints contain decoder state at each 2^SPREAD_LOG positions, which enables the decoder to jump to the closest checkpoint in constant time.

2. matches' offsets can be forced to align to a power of two, increasing the match range paying the price of unaligned matches.

3. optimal parser on compression side comes up with the best possible representation of the input.

4. chain-flattening can significantly reduce average number of match to match hops while sacrificing just 1-2% of the compression ratio.

When decompressing small slices (4-32 bytes), blaris significantly outperforms both heatshrink and tamp (500x for 1B reads). For bigger slices, since its decompression time depends linearly on the data, blaris performs worse, but it isn't really made for that.

And the best part, it is extremely lightweight in terms of memory. When compiled for RV32IMC architecture, it takes only 548-784 bytes of Flash memory, while using just 104-112B of SRAM regardless of the file size. For comparison, heatshrink is 1300-1464 bytes of Flash and uses 206-16594 bytes of SRAM depending on the window size, and tamp is 2238-3238 bytes of Flash while also using 520-16672 bytes of SRAM.

[1] https://github.com/atomicobject/heatshrink

[2] https://github.com/BrianPugh/tamp

title.value: Show HN: Blaris – Windowless Random-Access LZSS for Constrained Microcontrollers

story_text.value:
Howdy HN!

Inspired by StarSkirmish, I wanted to build a complex RTS that required you to bring your OWN agents and either play with them as allies, against them as enemies, or battle head-to-head with other agent-human pairs in public matches.

In AC you operate one or more planes (Orbit, Sky, Surface, Depths) of differing gameplay. As an old-school PC gamer I wanted the mechanics to resemble some of my favorite 90s games of yore: C&C, DungeonKeeper, Homeworld, StarCraft, and others. The idea is that you have specific objectives needed to maximize resource generation, aid in cross player support, and that a single plane cannot win independently.

Outside of gameplay, from an agentic tech pov, there are some other really cool things that come with this, including:

- A full specification + library to install agents into any game (http://playerthree.gg/) - A networking SDK for bidirectional agent communication - Symmetric maps - Deterministic simulation - Benchmarking tools - (soon) published benchmark data

Github: https://github.com/agent-command/agent-command Play now: https://agentcommand.gg/

Would love feedback and contribs if interested in RTS games and AI!

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

I've been software engineer for about 15 years. For me this industry was always about learning. To be honest, I don't feel this anymore. I see more and more people delegating most of their work to LLMs. We rarely talk about software design or architecture, because Claude is such a great companion, so most of the workers don't need these technical discussions.

Sometimes I feel a bit lost. I am not sure, what should I learn to stay in the industry and to have opportunity to work on interesting problems.

I always saw HN as a place full of ambitious and creatives people. Inspired by hackertube.org and hackerbooks.org, I scanned HN comments in 2026 to extract learning materials recommended by community here, to help me decide with the next steps in my learning journey.

Best, Mateusz

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

I was missing a (travel) planning tool that would let me plan at any detail level and start with a rough sketch. I wanted the flexibility to just put post-its on parts that are not planned (in detail) and a more detailed plan for other parts.

So I built a map that you can mark up with drawings, markers and post-its. Additionally you can link to different boards from markers to i.e. plan a city within a larger trip.

It's built using Maplibre, with self-hosted Protomaps for the tiles and Yjs for state. Currently, state is saved locally in the browser with no login and you can ex- and import your boards as json files. In the future I will want to add some form of collaboration and sync though.

I'm very curious to hear how it fits your (travel and non-travel) use case and what features you still need.

The code is open source (MPL-2.0) at https://github.com/bcye/mapboard
